content: Digital tracking systems, particularly those linked to uniquely identified individuals through electronic patient records, enable the registration and follow-up of patient services. These systems can be implemented using electronic medical records (EMRs) or other digital health record formats. The primary goal of digital tracking is to minimize disruptions in the continuity of care by ensuring timely follow-up interactions. Additionally, these systems may incorporate decision-support tools to assist healthcare workers in adhering to clinical protocols, scheduling future services, and managing cases effectively at the point of care. Digital tracking systems are often described as digital versions of paper-based registers for specific health domains. They include digitized registers for longitudinal health programs, such as tracking the health benefits and status of migrant populations, and case management logs for targeted populations. Decision-support tools for health workers are defined as digitized job aids that integrate an individual’s health information with the healthcare worker’s knowledge and clinical protocols. These tools assist in making accurate diagnostic and treatment decisions. A person-centered digital tracking and decision-support (DTDS) system is designed for use by healthcare workers at the point of care. It maintains a persistent record of health events and encounters, linking them to clinical decision-support systems to promote best practices. These systems also connect to reporting and management tools to enhance accountability. A DTDS record contains comprehensive information about an individual’s health status and the interventions provided, enabling the calculation of aggregate indicators for reporting and monitoring provider, stock, and system performance. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines recommending digital interventions to strengthen health systems and contribute to universal health coverage (UHC). For example, WHO recommends digital targeted client communication for health issues related to sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health, provided concerns about sensitive content and data privacy are addressed. Similarly, WHO supports the use of digital decision-support tools accessible via mobile devices for community and facility-based health workers, as long as these tasks fall within their defined scope of practice. WHO also recommends combining digital tracking of clients’ health status and services with decision-support tools in settings where the health system can support integrated implementation. This approach is recommended only in specific contexts and for tasks already defined within the health worker’s scope of practice. Additionally, WHO advocates for the digital provision of educational and training content to complement traditional methods of delivering continued health education and post-certification training. The concept of Digital Adaptation Kits (DAKs) aligns with the broader vision of SMART (Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable) Guidelines. These guidelines aim to maximize health impact by improving the fidelity and uptake of recommendations through a systematic process for transforming guideline development, delivery, and application. DAKs serve as a prerequisite for developing computable, machine-readable guidelines and executable reference software, as well as advanced analytics for precision health. DAKs are designed to provide a common language across various audiences, including maternal health program managers, software developers, and digital system implementers. They ensure adherence to WHO clinical, public health, and data use guidelines while facilitating consistency in health content. DAKs also enable health program leads and digital health teams to collaboratively understand and validate the health content within digital systems. They provide a starting point for core data elements and decision-support logic to be included in DTDS systems for specific health domains, such as antenatal care (ANC). The components of a DAK include health interventions and recommendations, generic personas, user scenarios, business processes and workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and reporting requirements, and functional and non-functional system requirements. These components are generic and need to be contextualized to local policies and requirements. For example, DAKs for antenatal care reflect workflows, data, and decision-support algorithms derived from WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience. DAKs also address technical considerations for self-care interventions from the perspective of health workers promoting these interventions to clients. They describe linkages to related services, such as managing intimate partner violence and addressing adolescent-specific considerations. While DAKs are generic, they must be adapted to reflect national policies and requirements. They have been developed for various health domains, including family planning, HIV, and STIs, and are being expanded to areas such as immunizations, postnatal care, and child health. The primary audience for DAKs includes health program managers within ministries of health, who work with digital health counterparts to determine health content requirements for DTDS systems. These managers oversee the implementation of clinical practices and policies within their health program areas. DAKs also support business analysts who bridge the gap between health content experts and software development teams. By providing key outputs such as data dictionaries and decision-support algorithms, DAKs ensure the validity and consistency of health content within DTDS systems.
